title: Agreed, Unread
passage:
When the consumer-law researcher Iris Hallenbeck timed a hundred volunteers as they signed up to an ordinary music app, the median time spent on the terms and conditions was eleven seconds. Long enough to find the button; not long enough to reach the second clause. Yet the behaviour was not carelessness. Asked afterwards, few of her volunteers could give any ___(1)___ of what they had just agreed to, and several said they had felt a flicker of guilt as they clicked. They had simply judged, correctly enough, that reading would have changed nothing.

___(2)___, the usual explanation blames length. The document in Hallenbeck's trial ran to nine thousand words, and a reader working at an ordinary pace would have needed the better part of an hour to reach the end of it. But her second experiment suggests that brevity alone is far from ___(3)___. When the same terms were rewritten as a single page of plain language, the median rose — to twenty-two seconds. People still did not read them. They merely felt worse about not reading them.

What the volunteers described, once Hallenbeck pressed them, was less ignorance than resignation. No private person has ever negotiated a clause of such a document; the choice on offer is the whole of it or none of the service, and everyone at the keyboard knows as much. To click, in those circumstances, is not to strike a bargain but to ___(4)___ that there was never one to strike. Consent obtained on those terms, she argues, is not a considered agreement at all but a ___(5)___ — a gesture that preserves the form of choice while quietly emptying it of content.

Hallenbeck stops well short of calling the practice deceptive. The firms disclose; the words are on the page; nobody is lied to. Her complaint is narrower and harder to answer. A legal system that treats the click as proof of an informed decision has long since stopped asking whether the decision was ever there to be made.
— Petra Vanterpool, consumer affairs

questions.rationale: Collocation gap; four singular abstract nouns, POS-uniform, all four shape-matched on -count/-cord. The frame 'few of her volunteers could give any ___ of what they had just agreed to' calls for the fixed phrase 'give an account of' (to describe or report something): 'account' locks, and the sense — they could not report the contents — is exactly what the sentence needs. accord = collocation_misfit; 'accord' is thematically tempting because the paragraph is about agreeing to something, but 'give any accord of' is not English (an accord is a settlement between parties, and the noun does not take 'give ... of'). discount = collocation_misfit; a consumer-commerce word that fits the topic's furniture but not the frame — 'give any discount of what they had agreed to' collapses into nonsense. recount = collocation_misfit; the noun 'recount' means a second counting of votes, never a retelling, so 'give any recount of' fails on sense even though the verb 'recount' would be near-synonymous. Only 'account' both collocates with 'give ... of' and carries the required meaning.

Connective gap; four sentence-initial adverbs of the same connective class. The gapped sentence introduces the obvious, expected account of the problem ('the usual explanation blames length'), which the paragraph then overturns at 'But her second experiment suggests...'. The slot therefore needs an expectation marker that grants the received view before it is qualified: 'Naturally' ('as one would expect') is the only fit. Consequently = wrong_logic; it asserts cause and effect, but the preceding sentence (the volunteers judged that reading would change nothing) is not a cause of which the length explanation is the effect. Conversely = wrong_logic; 'conversely' claims that the new statement inverts the terms of the one before it, but this sentence does not invert the volunteers' reasoning — it sets the conventional account of the same behaviour beside it, and the paragraph's real reversal arrives one sentence later at 'But', which a contrast marker here would leave contradicting a contrast. Ultimately = wrong_logic; it marks a final upshot, whereas the length explanation is the paragraph's starting position and is the very thing the passage goes on to reject. Only 'Naturally' sets up the granted expectation that the later 'But' answers.

Polarity gap with a suffix-rhymed -ive adjective set. 'Far from X' inverts polarity: whatever fills the gap is what brevity is NOT. The evidence that follows — shortening the terms to a single page moved the median from eleven seconds to twenty-two, and 'People still did not read them' — shows that shortness settles nothing, so the gap must hold the positive-pole word 'decisive' ('far from decisive' = nowhere near settling the matter). ineffective = polarity_mirror; a skimmer who has registered the negative finding grabs the negative-sounding word, but 'far from ineffective' would assert that brevity worked well, which contradicts the very result being reported. dismissive = sense misfit; it describes an attitude a person takes, and brevity is a property of a document, not a stance. excessive = sense misfit; 'excessive brevity' is ordinary English (too terse), so the block is not grammar but relevance — whether the rewritten terms were too short was never the question, and 'far from excessive' would say nothing about whether shortening helped. Only 'decisive' survives the inversion the frame imposes.

Collocation gap with a suffix-rhymed -cede verb set. The frame 'is not to strike a bargain but to ___ that there was never one to strike' requires a verb that takes a that-clause and means to admit something unwelcome: 'concede that' locks, and it carries the paragraph's argument (clicking admits the absence of any real bargain). accede = collocation_misfit; the verb is thematically tempting because it means to agree, but it is intransitive with 'to' ('accede to a demand') and cannot govern a that-clause. precede = sense misfit; it means to come before in order or time and takes a direct object, not a that-clause. recede = sense misfit; it is intransitive and describes something moving back or growing fainter, which is not something a click can do to a proposition. Only 'concede' has both the complement pattern and the meaning the frame demands.

Collocation gap with a suffix-rhymed -ity noun set. The frame 'is not a considered agreement at all but a ___', glossed immediately by 'a gesture that preserves the form of choice while quietly emptying it of content', calls for the countable idiom 'a formality' — something done because the procedure requires it, not because it decides anything. finality = sense misfit; 'a finality' does occur in English ('there was a finality in her voice'), so the block is meaning rather than grammar: finality is the quality of settling a matter for good, the opposite of what the appositive describes — a gesture that empties choice of content settles nothing. neutrality = sense misfit; the passage is describing an empty ritual, not an absence of taking sides, and 'a neutrality' is not idiomatic as a count noun for a thing done. banality = sense misfit; a banality is a trite remark or platitude, which a click is not, though the word is tempting because the passage calls the act routine. Only 'formality' names an empty procedural act, which is exactly what the appositive gloss spells out.
